--- title: "Hyperparameter selection" description: "Finding the bottom of the U-curve without spending your test set, and how unstable that choice really is." order: 6 categories: [generalisation, tuning] --- ## The setting every page has left open Every page in this section has ended in the same place. There is a setting, tree depth or λ or `minbucket`, with a best value, and the best value cannot be read off the training data because the training curve has no minimum. Each page has also cheated, choosing the setting by looking at the test set, and said so. This page stops cheating. It is the procedural heart of applied machine learning: how to choose the knob honestly, what tidymodels calls the pieces, and, the part usually left out, how much that choice moves if you had sampled different stations. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the data on this page The coastal survey used here is **simulated**, not a real survey. That is deliberate: because we wrote the generating process (`R/make-example-data.R`), we know the true relationships and can show whether a model recovers them. No real survey is being misrepresented, and the figures are not results about any real species. See `data/README.md` for what is built into it. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the Python tabs Most code blocks on this page have an **R** and a **Python** tab, and picking one switches the whole page. The R tab is what produced the tables and figures you see; the Python tab is the scikit-learn equivalent, shown for translation rather than executed by the site. Figures stay in R throughout, and a few steps with no scikit-learn counterpart have no Python tab, which is itself worth noticing. It is real code, not pseudocode: it runs against the same files through `python/mlbasic_data.py`, and `python/check-snippets.py` executes every snippet in the site to keep it honest. Expect the **numbers to differ slightly**: R and Python draw their random splits from different generators, so the split is not the same one. The conclusions are. ::: ## The idea A **hyperparameter** is a setting fixed before fitting, which the fitting cannot choose because its job is to constrain the fitting. Tree depth, the number of neighbours in k-NN, λ in ridge, the learning rate in boosting. Parameters are learned; hyperparameters are selected. Selecting them needs data the model has not been fitted to. There are two ways to get it. **A validation split.** Divide the training data again: fit on one part, score on the other, choose the setting with the best score. Simple, and it wastes data and depends heavily on which stations happened to fall in the validation part. **k-fold cross-validation.** Divide the training data into *k* parts. Fit on *k*−1 and score on the remaining one, *k* times, so every station is scored exactly once by a model that did not see it. Average the *k* scores. Nothing is wasted, and the average is far steadier, and that steadiness is measured below. So the split is three-way: | Data | Used for | How often | | --- | --- | --- | | Training folds | Fitting parameters | Every candidate setting | | Held-out fold | Choosing hyperparameters | Every candidate setting | | **Test set** | Estimating performance | **Once, at the very end** | The test set is spent the first time you look at it and adjust. There is no way to unspend it, which is why it is set aside in [section 2](../02-marine-data/splitting-data.qmd) before any modelling happens. ## Worked example ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} survey <- load_coastal_survey_clean() set.seed(506) d <- survey |> select(abundance, depth_m, temperature_c, chlorophyll_mg_m3, salinity_psu, substrate, season) |> drop_na() split <- initial_split(d, prop = 0.75) train <- training(split) test <- testing(split) folds <- vfold_cv(train, v = 10) c(folds = nrow(folds), fitted_on = nrow(analysis(folds$splits[[1]])), scored_on = nrow(assessment(folds$splits[[1]]))) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> folds fitted_on scored_on #> 10 486 54 ``` ::: ::: ## Python ```python import numpy as np import pandas as pd from sklearn.model_selection import GridSearchCV, KFold, train_test_split from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeRegressor from mlbasic_data import load_coastal_survey_clean survey = load_coastal_survey_clean() columns = ["abundance", "depth_m", "temperature_c", "chlorophyll_mg_m3", "salinity_psu", "substrate", "season"] d = pd.get_dummies(survey[columns].dropna(), drop_first=True) train, test = train_test_split(d, train_size=0.75, random_state=506) features = [c for c in d.columns if c != "abundance"] X_train, y_train = train[features], train["abundance"] X_test, y_test = test[features], test["abundance"] folds = KFold(n_splits=10, shuffle=True, random_state=506) first_train, first_test = next(folds.split(X_train)) pd.Series({"folds": folds.get_n_splits(), "fitted_on": len(first_train), "scored_on": len(first_test)}) ``` ::: A tree with two hyperparameters to choose: how deep it may grow, and how many stations a node needs before it may split. `tune()` marks each as a value to be filled in later. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} tree_spec <- decision_tree( tree_depth = tune(), min_n = tune(), cost_complexity = 0 ) |> set_engine("rpart") |> set_mode("regression") tree_workflow <- workflow() |> add_formula(abundance ~ .) |> add_model(tree_spec) grid <- expand_grid( tree_depth = c(2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12), min_n = c(2, 5, 10, 20, 40, 80) ) tuned <- tune_grid(tree_workflow, resamples = folds, grid = grid, metrics = metric_set(rmse)) collect_metrics(tuned) |> arrange(mean) |> select(tree_depth, min_n, mean, std_err) |> slice_head(n = 6) |> mutate(across(c(mean, std_err), \(x) round(x, 4))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| tree_depth| min_n| mean| std_err| |----------:|-----:|------:|-------:| | 3| 10| 4.4824| 0.1867| | 3| 80| 4.5206| 0.2357| | 4| 80| 4.5213| 0.2479| | 4| 10| 4.5289| 0.1957| | 6| 80| 4.5372| 0.2383| | 8| 80| 4.5372| 0.2383|
::: ::: ## Python ```python grid = {"max_depth": [2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12], "min_samples_split": [2, 5, 10, 20, 40, 80]} # cost_complexity = 0 is ccp_alpha = 0: no pruning, so the two knobs above are # the only thing holding the tree back. tuned = GridSearchCV( DecisionTreeRegressor(ccp_alpha=0.0, random_state=506), param_grid=grid, scoring="neg_root_mean_squared_error", cv=folds, ).fit(X_train, y_train) # GridSearchCV reports the standard deviation across folds; the standard error # tidymodels prints is that divided by the root of the number of folds. metrics = pd.DataFrame({ "tree_depth": tuned.cv_results_["param_max_depth"], "min_n": tuned.cv_results_["param_min_samples_split"], "mean": -tuned.cv_results_["mean_test_score"], "std_err": tuned.cv_results_["std_test_score"] / np.sqrt(folds.get_n_splits()), }) metrics.sort_values("mean").head(6).round(4) ``` ::: Thirty-six candidate settings, each scored on ten folds, so 360 model fits, which is why tuning is the expensive step. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} surface <- collect_metrics(tuned) best <- select_best(tuned, metric = "rmse") ggplot(surface, aes(factor(min_n), factor(tree_depth), fill = mean)) + geom_tile(colour = "white", linewidth = 0.6) + geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.2f", mean)), size = 3, colour = if_else(surface$mean > 5, "white", "grey15")) + geom_tile(data = best, fill = NA, colour = "black", linewidth = 1) + scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "mako", direction = -1, breaks = c(4.5, 5.0, 5.5)) + labs(x = "min_n: stations required to split a node", y = "tree_depth", fill = "CV RMSE", title = "Most of this grid is a tie", subtitle = "Outlined: the best cell. Ten-fold cross-validation on 540 stations.") + theme(panel.grid.major = element_blank()) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Cross-validated RMSE across the grid of tree depth and minimum node size. The best cell is 4.482, at depth 3 with min_n = 10. The surface is almost flat across most of the grid; only the deep, small-node corner at the top left, where the tree is allowed to grow to depth 8 or 12 with nodes of 2 to 10 stations, is clearly bad.](hyperparameter-selection_files/figure-html/fig-surface-1.png){#fig-surface fig-alt='A grid of tiles with minimum node size on the horizontal axis at values 2, 5, 10, 20, 40 and 80, and tree depth on the vertical axis at 2, 3, 4, 6, 8 and 12 running upward. Each tile is shaded by cross-validated RMSE and labelled with its value. Most tiles read between 4.48 and 4.73 and are shaded a similar pale green. Five tiles in the top-left corner, depth 8 and 12 at node sizes 2, 5 and 10, are distinctly darker, reading 5.06, 5.09, 5.16, 5.59 and 5.76. The best tile, 4.48, sits at depth 3 and node size 10 and is outlined in black.' width=1400} ::: ::: How many of the thirty-six settings are genuinely distinguishable from the winner? ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} one_se <- select_by_one_std_err(tuned, metric = "rmse", tree_depth, desc(min_n)) best_row <- collect_metrics(tuned) |> slice_min(mean, n = 1) c(`settings within one SE of the best` = sum(collect_metrics(tuned)$mean <= best_row$mean + best_row$std_err), `grid points` = nrow(grid)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> settings within one SE of the best grid points #> 19 36 ``` ::: ::: ## Python ```python best_row = metrics.loc[metrics["mean"].idxmin()] within = metrics["mean"] <= best_row["mean"] + best_row["std_err"] pd.Series({"settings within one SE of the best": int(within.sum()), "grid points": len(metrics)}) ``` ::: ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} one_se |> select(tree_depth, min_n) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| tree_depth| min_n| |----------:|-----:| | 2| 20|
::: ::: ## Python ```python # scikit-learn has no select_by_one_std_err(): the rule is a sort over the # settings that tie, simplest first: shallow trees, then large nodes. one_se = (metrics[within] .sort_values(["tree_depth", "min_n"], ascending=[True, False]) .iloc[0]) one_se[["tree_depth", "min_n"]] ``` ::: ### Finalising, and spending the test set once ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} final_fit <- tree_workflow |> finalize_workflow(best) |> last_fit(split, metrics = metric_set(rmse, rsq, mae)) collect_metrics(final_fit) |> select(.metric, .estimate) |> mutate(.estimate = round(.estimate, 4)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|.metric | .estimate| |:-------|---------:| |rmse | 4.4646| |rsq | 0.1076| |mae | 3.1073|
::: ::: ## Python ```python from sklearn.metrics import (mean_absolute_error, r2_score, root_mean_squared_error) # last_fit(): refit at the chosen setting on all the training data, then score # once on the test set that tuning never saw. GridSearchCV has already done the # refitting, at its own best setting. final_fit = tuned.best_estimator_ predicted = final_fit.predict(X_test) pd.DataFrame({ ".metric": ["rmse", "rsq", "mae"], ".estimate": [ root_mean_squared_error(y_test, predicted), r2_score(y_test, predicted), mean_absolute_error(y_test, predicted), ], }).round(4) ``` ::: `last_fit()` is the only function in this section that touches the test set. It refits the chosen workflow on the whole training set and scores it on the test set, once. Everything before it used cross-validation. ### The reliability of the choice The CV surface picks depth 3 and `min_n` 10. To see whether that is a finding, we repeat the selection with a single validation split, the simpler procedure, forty times, each time with a different random split of the same training data. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} rmse_of <- function(observed, predicted) sqrt(mean((observed - predicted)^2)) set.seed(61) winners <- map_dfr(1:40, \(r) { rows <- sample(nrow(train), round(0.75 * nrow(train))) inner_train <- train[rows, ] validation <- train[-rows, ] errors <- pmap_dbl(grid, \(tree_depth, min_n) { fit <- rpart(abundance ~ ., data = inner_train, control = rpart.control(cp = 0, maxdepth = tree_depth, minsplit = min_n, minbucket = ceiling(min_n / 3))) rmse_of(validation$abundance, predict(fit, validation)) }) grid[which.min(errors), ] |> mutate(replicate = r, winning_rmse = min(errors)) }) c(`distinct winning settings` = nrow(distinct(winners, tree_depth, min_n)), `grid points` = nrow(grid)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> distinct winning settings grid points #> 16 36 ``` ::: ::: ## Python ```python from sklearn.model_selection import ParameterGrid settings = list(ParameterGrid(grid)) rng = np.random.default_rng(61) def winner_of_one_split(): rows = rng.choice(len(train), round(0.75 * len(train)), replace=False) held = np.setdiff1d(np.arange(len(train)), rows) inner, validation = train.iloc[rows], train.iloc[held] errors = [ root_mean_squared_error( validation["abundance"], DecisionTreeRegressor(ccp_alpha=0.0, random_state=506, **setting) .fit(inner[features], inner["abundance"]) .predict(validation[features])) for setting in settings ] k = int(np.argmin(errors)) return {"tree_depth": settings[k]["max_depth"], "min_n": settings[k]["min_samples_split"], "winning_rmse": errors[k]} winners = pd.DataFrame([winner_of_one_split() for _ in range(40)]) pd.Series({ "distinct winning settings": len(winners[["tree_depth", "min_n"]].drop_duplicates()), "grid points": len(settings), }) ``` ::: ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} winners |> count(tree_depth, min_n, sort = TRUE) |> slice_head(n = 6) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| tree_depth| min_n| n| |----------:|-----:|--:| | 3| 5| 5| | 3| 20| 4| | 3| 80| 4| | 3| 2| 3| | 3| 10| 3| | 4| 2| 3|
::: ::: ## Python ```python (winners.value_counts(["tree_depth", "min_n"]) .reset_index(name="n") .head(6)) ``` ::: ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} c(lowest_claimed = min(winners$winning_rmse), highest_claimed = max(winners$winning_rmse), sd = sd(winners$winning_rmse)) |> round(3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> lowest_claimed highest_claimed sd #> 3.361 5.526 0.451 ``` ::: ::: ## Python ```python pd.Series({ "lowest_claimed": winners["winning_rmse"].min(), "highest_claimed": winners["winning_rmse"].max(), "sd": winners["winning_rmse"].std(), }).round(3) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} p1 <- winners |> count(tree_depth, min_n) |> right_join(grid, by = c("tree_depth", "min_n")) |> mutate(n = replace_na(n, 0)) |> ggplot(aes(factor(min_n), factor(tree_depth), fill = n)) + geom_tile(colour = "white", linewidth = 0.6) + scale_fill_gradient(low = "#f2f5f7", high = ml_palette[["vermilion"]]) + labs(x = "min_n", y = "tree_depth", fill = "times\nchosen", title = "Where the winner landed") + theme(panel.grid.major = element_blank()) p2 <- ggplot(winners, aes(winning_rmse)) + geom_histogram(bins = 14, fill = ml_palette[["blue"]], colour = "white") + labs(x = "Validation RMSE of the chosen setting", y = "Splits", title = "And what it claimed to score") p1 + p2 ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Which grid cell wins, across forty different single validation splits of the same training data. Sixteen of the thirty-six cells win at least once, spanning the full range of both hyperparameters. The reported score of the winner ranges from 3.36 to 5.53, a spread of more than two individuals, caused entirely by which stations landed in the validation set.](hyperparameter-selection_files/figure-html/fig-instability-1.png){#fig-instability fig-alt='Two panels. The left panel is a grid of tiles matching the tuning surface, shaded by how many of forty validation splits chose each cell; sixteen cells are shaded at all, scattered across the whole grid rather than clustered, and the darkest cell was chosen five times. The right panel is a histogram of the winning validation RMSE across the forty splits, spread from 3.4 to 5.5 with a broad peak near 4.4.' width=1600} ::: ::: ## Most of the grid is a tie **Most of the grid is a tie.** The best cross-validated RMSE is 4.482 with a standard error of 0.187. Nineteen of the thirty-six settings are within one standard error of it. "Depth 3 with `min_n` 10 is optimal" is not supportable; what the data supports is "keep the tree shallow, and do not let nodes get small". **A single validation split chooses almost at random.** Forty splits of the same training data produced **sixteen different winners**, using every depth from 2 to 8 and every node size from 2 to 80, the entire grid range on both axes. The winning setting's own reported RMSE ranged from 3.36 to 5.53. If you tune with one validation split and report the validation score, you are reporting the best of thirty-six noisy numbers and calling it performance. Cross-validation does not remove this, but it averages ten estimates instead of one, and the effect on stability is large. This is the whole argument for *k*-fold, and it is worth the tenfold computing cost. **The 1-SE rule.** When many settings tie, the convention is to take the *simplest* one within one standard error of the best rather than the best itself. Here that is depth 2 with `min_n` 20, a tree you could print on a postcard, chosen on the grounds that the more elaborate model's advantage is not distinguishable from noise and simpler models generalise more safely. It is a convention, not a theorem, and worth applying deliberately rather than by default. **And tuning bought very little here.** The tuned tree scores 4.463 on the test set. Predicting the training mean at every station scores 4.492. Careful ten-fold tuning of a tree over thirty-six settings improved on using no predictors at all by 0.6%. That is not a failure of the procedure. It is the [bias–variance page's](bias-variance.qmd) finding arriving in practice: the irreducible noise in these counts dwarfs what any model can extract, so the room tuning has to work in is narrow. The procedure is still correct, and on a problem with more signal, or with the penalised models of [the previous page](regularisation.qmd) where the untuned fit scored 7.41 against 4.64, the same machinery is worth a great deal. ::: {.callout-warning} The CV score of the *selected* setting is optimistic as an estimate of that setting's performance, because it is the minimum of thirty-six noisy numbers. Here CV said 4.482 and the test set said 4.463, so the bias is invisible against the noise of one 180-station test set, but it is real, and it grows with the size of the grid. This is why a test set held back from tuning is not optional, and why [section 7](../07-validation/index.qmd) covers nested resampling for the cases where you cannot afford one. ::: ### Searching a larger space A regular grid costs the product of its axes. Two hyperparameters at six values each is 36 settings; four at six values is 1,296, times ten folds. Two standard escapes: ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Regular grid: every combination. Fine for one or two hyperparameters. grid_regular(tree_depth(), min_n(), levels = 6) # Space-filling: spreads points to cover the space evenly. Much better once # you have three or more hyperparameters, at the same computational budget. grid_space_filling( trees(range = c(200, 1500)), learn_rate(range = c(-3, -0.5)), tree_depth(range = c(2, 10)), loss_reduction(), size = 40 ) ``` ::: ## Python ```python from scipy.stats import qmc from sklearn.model_selection import ParameterGrid # Regular grid: every combination. Fine for one or two hyperparameters. pd.DataFrame(ParameterGrid({"tree_depth": [1, 4, 8, 11, 15], "min_n": [2, 11, 21, 30, 40]})).head() # Space-filling: spreads points to cover the space evenly. Much better once # you have three or more hyperparameters, at the same computational budget. # scikit-learn has no grid_space_filling(); scipy's qmc module is the tool. design = qmc.scale( qmc.LatinHypercube(d=4, rng=np.random.default_rng(1)).random(40), l_bounds=[200, -3, 2, -10], # trees, log10 learning rate, u_bounds=[1500, -0.5, 10, 1.5], # tree depth, log10 loss reduction ) pd.DataFrame({ "trees": design[:, 0].round(), "learn_rate": (10 ** design[:, 1]).round(5), "tree_depth": design[:, 2].round(), "loss_reduction": (10 ** design[:, 3]).round(5), }).head() ``` ::: Space-filling designs win for a reason worth knowing: hyperparameters differ enormously in how much they matter, and a regular grid wastes most of its evaluations re-testing the ones that do not. Forty well-spread points usually beat a 1,296-point grid on the same budget. ## Limits of this tuning **Tuning on cross-validation, then reporting the cross-validation score, is circular.** The resampling was used to choose; it can no longer be used to estimate. The fix is a held-out test set, as above, or **nested resampling**, an inner loop that tunes and an outer loop that estimates, which [section 7](../07-validation/index.qmd) covers. **Every preprocessing step must go inside the resampling.** Imputing, centring, selecting variables or balancing classes on the whole training set before cross-validating leaks information from each held-out fold into the model that will score it. `recipe()` inside a `workflow()` exists precisely to prevent this, and it is why [section 2](../02-marine-data/information-leakage.qmd) insisted on recipes over `mutate()`. **Random k-fold is wrong for this dataset.** These 720 stations come from 160 repeatedly visited sites, so ordinary `vfold_cv()` puts visits to the same site in both the training and the held-out fold. The tuning above is therefore optimistic in a way this page cannot fix. `group_vfold_cv()` and `spatial_block_cv()` can, and [section 7](../07-validation/index.qmd) is where they belong. **A winning hyperparameter is not a scientific result.** Depth 3 beat depth 4 by 0.05 on this survey. Nothing follows from that about trees, about this species, or about the next survey. The tuned value is a setting, not a finding, and it should be reported as one. ::: {.callout-tip} ## Key points - Hyperparameters need data the model was not fitted to. Use cross-validation on the training set, and keep the test set for one final measurement. - The tidymodels route is `tune()` → `vfold_cv()` → `tune_grid()` → `select_best()` → `finalize_workflow()` → `last_fit()`. Only the last touches the test set. - **The choice is much less certain than it looks.** Nineteen of thirty-six settings were within one standard error of the best, and forty single validation splits picked sixteen different winners spanning the whole grid. - Prefer the **simplest setting within one standard error** of the best. - Tuning is worth what the signal allows: 0.6% over the mean for this tree, against a 37% improvement for penalised regression on the previous page. ::: ## Try it yourself 1. Re-run the instability experiment using `vfold_cv(v = 5)` inside each replicate instead of a single validation split. How many distinct winners now, and how much does the spread of winning scores narrow? 2. Swap `vfold_cv()` for `group_vfold_cv(group = site_id)`; you will need to keep `site_id` in the data. Does the chosen tree get simpler or more complex, and why should honest resampling push it in that direction?
